claims.text: Progressive creep deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is primarily governed by interface-mediated mechanisms.
Increasing interfacial lattice distortion promotes localized enhanced atomic diffusion.
Increasing interfacial compositional gradients promotes localized enhanced atomic diffusion.
Increasing interfacial lattice distortion and compositional gradients facilitates dislocation climb.
Interfaces with increased lattice distortion and compositional gradients accelerate creep relative to chemically homogeneous interfaces.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers inherently exhibit lattice distortion.
Nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers possess local short-range order at their interfaces.
Adjusting interface chemistry and layer thickness can systematically modulate interfacial lattice distortion.
Adjusting interface chemistry and layer thickness can systematically modulate interfacial short-range order.
Higher temperature and stress accelerate creep by increasing atomic rearrangement, diffusion, and activation of deformation carriers.
Severe lattice distortion at chemically complex interfaces lowers the barrier to creep deformation through enhanced diffusion or dislocation climb.
Bulk dislocation glide and interface-localized processes jointly control creep in these multilayers.
More highly distorted interfaces will produce an earlier onset of creep than homogeneous interfaces.
More highly distorted interfaces will increase strain localization at interfaces.
More highly distorted interfaces will produce higher overall creep strain rates.
The proposed interface-mediated mechanism will dominate when the nanoscale architecture is retained and temperature is high enough to activate diffusion.
Interfacial-distortion effects may be negligible below a critical distortion threshold.
